This is my first post using [Nikola](http://getnikola.com/), a static website generator.

Shortly after I started at NYU I put up a website using [Drupal](http://drupal.org/). I created a theme based on the department's website by reading a lot of HTML source and reverse engineering.

I wanted to make it look like the department's site so that it wouldn't look like I had dropped in the latest CMS with its snazzy default theme. The natural order of website theme popularity is:

1.  A site comes out with a radically different design. Everyone who reads the site likes the style and dreams of having their content look like that.
2.  Someone makes it easy to produce websites that look the same way. People's dreams come true.
3.  There goes the neighborhood: lots of low-quality websites pop up in the same style as the new one, tarnishing the appeal of the design.

I have seen this happen with [Slashdot](http://slashdot.org/), PHP-Nuke, [WordPress](http://www.wordpress.org/), [MediaWiki](http://www.mediawiki.org/) (i.e., Wikipedia), and more.

The trouble was that I didn't really like the department's website that much (I still don't like it that much, but we have at least updated the colors and the use of CSS). So I although my plan was faithfully executed, I was dissatisfied.

The other thing I discovered was that I didn't have a lot of time to be a website manager, let alone a database admin. I didn't want to undertake the multistep process of backing up, downloading new code, uploading, running update scripts, etc. I was probaby leaving some security holes open because I didn't religiously update whenvever emergench bugfixes came out.

So my energy to work on my website sputtered. Then I heard that 75% of the websites in the US use WordPress. That seems to have been a made-up statistic, but it made me think again about adopting it. I had to create a new website for a program I run, so I picked GSTEM for the CMS.

What I discovered there was that WordPress can be confusing to manage too, especially if you don't do it that often. And, either our department throttles database traffic for small faculty websites, or WordPress is slow for my needs. So I never got around to migrating.

Finally I've got some impetus to work more on my website. Most of my colleagues have much better websites, and it's not because (as they would admit, I'm sure) they know more about web programming than me. It's that they don't worry about it, and just put up their content.

I was also inspired by the workshop at AIM I attended last week about a document workflow for math textbooks based on XML. Having clean source and scripts to generate fancy markup was something I toyed with many years ago. I also remembered talk about [Jekyll](http://jekyllrb.org/) and that got me looking around for static site generators. This is how I found Nikola.

What I need from a website:

- easy editing: A static site makes it harder to edit pages on-the-fly via the web. But I can usually wait until I get to a terminal. Also, if the site can track me on Twitter or other social media sites I may not need to edit posts or pages on the go.
- Reliable updating: if the update process takes too long, I will put it off. Since updating take precedence over writing, writing gets put off too. Result: no new content.
- content capabilities:
  - I want to be able to include math with MathJAX. Having spent a lot of time on the [Math Stackexchange](http://math.stackexchange.com/) I don't want to put math up any other way.
  - Also, I'll want to write about code in the languages I use: LaTeX, python, shell, Mathematica, and more.
  - Finally, I can imagine some pages to be generated from an automatic process from other source files. For instance, a script that parses my calendar and looks for my next "office Hours". Or an XML CV that can be processed into html and PDF. This would encourage me to keep my CV up-to-date.
- Links to other departmental pages. That shouldn't be hard in any CMS.
- styling. I won't make the mistake I made last time, which took a lot of work to generate a site that didn't look special. I want the site to look like the department's (new) site, so that visitors don't feel like they've strayed too far off the beaten path. But I also want to look like I've spend time on it to make it look nice, in order to showcase my skills in that area (such as they are).

So we'll see how it goes with Nikola. I'm going to put these pages in a temporary place and see how it works with writing. If I'm sucessful I'll spend the summer migrating the Drupal site over to WordPress, then importing into Nikola. Hopefully by the fall I'll having something that I won't be embarassed about.
